section_1.title: Geometric Interpretation: The Intersection of Worlds
section_1.content: Introduce linear systems as the intersection of lines/planes. Use a 2D coordinate system where two linear equations represent two lines. Emphasize that the solution is the point where they cross (or the line if they are identical).
section_1.example: Visualizing two paths of 'Robot A' and 'Robot B'; where their paths cross is the unique solution coordinate (x, y).

section_2.title: The Inverse Matrix: The 'Undo' Button
section_2.content: Explain the inverse matrix as the transformation that reverses a linear operation. If matrix A maps a vector to a new position, A⁻¹ maps it back to the origin state. Prerequisite: Understanding matrix-vector multiplication as a transformation.
section_2.example: A 'Spatial Teleporter' device: Matrix A moves a cat from Point A to Point B; the inverse matrix A⁻¹ acts as the 'Return Home' button to bring the cat back.

section_3.title: Column Space: The Reach of a Transformation
section_3.content: Define column space as the span of the column vectors. It represents all possible destinations (output space) reachable by the matrix transformation. Visualize this as a 'reachable region' on the 2D/3D plane.
section_3.example: A 'Paint Brush' robot: The column space represents the total area on the canvas the robot can cover given its two mechanical arm vectors.

section_4.title: Null Space: The 'Ghost' Zone
section_4.content: Define null space as the set of vectors that the matrix collapses to the zero vector. Visualize this as the 'Kernel'—what gets 'deleted' or flattened by the transformation.
section_4.example: A 'Magic Lens': Anything placed inside the null space zone of the lens becomes invisible (mapped to zero) when viewed through the lens.

section_5.title: Synthesis & Summary
section_5.content: Connect the concepts: If a matrix has an inverse, the column space spans the whole room and the null space contains only the origin point. Review the interplay between geometry and algebra.
section_5.example: A 'Dimensional Map': A square matrix is like a complete map (invertible); a singular matrix is like a map folded flat into a line (losing information in the null space).
